sections.title: What Word is for, and how to start it

blocks.html:
Microsoft Word is a program for writing documents: letters, lists, notes, community notices, and other pages made mostly of words. Canada’s Skills for Success names Word as one of the common digital tools people use to complete a task (alongside other programs such as Excel). This course stays with Word. Number tables that calculate belong in *Microsoft Excel Basics*. Everyday device skills such as the Start menu itself are covered more fully in *Everyday Computers and Smartphones*. Workplace tone and longer writing craft belong in *Workplace Writing*. Resumes go deeper in *Job Search*.

To start Word on a Windows computer, Microsoft’s steps are: click the Start button, or press the Windows key, to open the Start menu; find Word in the list of applications; then click it. Microsoft says the startup screen appears and Word starts. The first time you start Word, a licence agreement might appear. Follow the on-screen choices with help from a tutor if you need it.

If you see recent files or template choices on the startup screen, look for a blank document if that option is there. Screens differ by version and by whether you are using desktop Word or Word for the web. This course teaches the desktop steps Microsoft publishes. Ask a tutor rather than guessing at a reset or an upgrade.

You do not need to buy a new computer. A library or council machine with Word is a valid place to practise. On a shared computer, use a practice file — not someone else’s letter.

sections.title: A tour of the Word window

blocks.html:
Microsoft’s tour of the Word window names eight parts that are useful from the first day.

The title bar at the top shows the file name of the document you are editing and the name of the software. It also includes the usual Minimize, Restore, and Close buttons. The Quick Access Toolbar holds frequent commands such as Save, Undo, and Redo. A small menu at the end of that toolbar lets you add other commands if you want to later — you do not need to customise it today.

The File tab is the place for commands that act on the document itself rather than on the words inside it. Microsoft lists New, Open, Save As, Print, and Close there. The ribbon is the wide strip of tools you use while writing. Microsoft notes that the ribbon’s appearance changes with the size of the monitor: Word may compress or rearrange the controls on a smaller screen. The Home tab on the ribbon is where you will find most everyday text formatting in later lessons.

The large white edit window shows the contents of the document. A scroll bar moves your view up or down. The status bar at the bottom shows information about the document. A zoom slider changes how large the page looks on screen without changing the printed size of the words. If the page looks tiny on a library monitor, try zoom before you change the font.

sections.title: File, ribbon, and how to leave without a scare

blocks.html:
It helps to keep two ideas apart. The File tab looks after the whole file: starting a new document, opening one you saved, saving a copy, printing, or closing. The ribbon looks after the words and the look of the page: fonts, styles, and (on other tabs) pictures or page setup. If you cannot find Bold, you are probably not on the Home tab. If you cannot find Print, look under File.

To quit Word, Microsoft says to click the X in the upper-right corner of the screen. If you changed the document since the last save, a message asks whether you want to save. Click Yes to save, No to quit without saving, or Cancel if you clicked X by mistake and want to stay. That Cancel choice is a kindness: it means you can back out of leaving. Lesson 3 will teach you how to save on purpose so you are not relying on that last-second question.

This course is not MOS training and not a promise of a job. The goal today is simpler: start Word, recognise the window, and leave without panic. Write down any new word — ribbon, File tab, edit window — and ask if a label on your screen does not match this lesson.

sections.title: Type, and press Enter only when you mean a new paragraph

blocks.html:
Click in the white edit window and start typing. Word wraps the text to the next line when you reach the end of a line, so you do not need to press Enter at the end of every line. Press Enter when you want a new paragraph — a greeting on its own line, a blank line before a new idea, or the start of a list you will format in Lesson 4.

Type slowly at first. If letters appear in the wrong place, click where you want them and try again. The cursor (a blinking line) shows where the next letter will go. Backspace deletes to the left of the cursor. If you are using an on-screen keyboard on a tablet that has Word, tap in the page first so the cursor appears, then type — the same idea as tapping a box before you type on a phone.

Use Canadian spelling as you practise, such as *centre*, *colour*, and *cheque*. You will ask Word to check spelling in Lesson 7. Do not type passwords, SINs, bank numbers, or other private details into a practice file on a shared computer. Write about your week, a greeting, or the sample sentences in the practice document instead.

If the page looks too small or too large, use the zoom control from Lesson 1. Zoom changes only how large the page looks; it does not change the printed size of the words.

sections.title: Select text before you change it

blocks.html:
Microsoft says that before you edit or format text, you must first select it. The steps are: place the cursor at the beginning of the text you want to change; press and hold the left mouse button; then move the mouse to the right (Microsoft calls this dragging). A background colour appears on the selected words so you can see the range. Then you can delete the selection, type replacement words, or apply formatting (Lesson 4). To remove the selection, click once somewhere else on the page.

On a trackpad, the same idea holds: press and drag across the words. If you drag too far, keep the button down and move back, or click away and try again. Selecting a whole paragraph is easier if you start just before the first word.

A common mix-up is to click Bold or another button with nothing selected. Then Word may wait to apply the look to the next letters you type, or it may seem to do nothing. The habit that saves time is: select first, then choose the command. If you selected too much, click once on the page to clear the highlight and drag again. You do not need keyboard shortcuts to select text today; dragging is the method Microsoft’s new-user guide describes. A tutor can show extra tricks later if your hands find dragging hard. On a shared computer, select only your own practice words — never someone else’s letter that happens to be open.

sections.title: Undo and redo are everyday safety nets

blocks.html:
Microsoft says you can undo, redo, or repeat many actions in Word. To undo, press Ctrl+Z or select Undo on the Quick Access Toolbar. You can use Undo (or Ctrl+Z) more than once to step backward. To undo several actions at the same time, Microsoft says you can select the arrow next to Undo, choose the actions in the list, then select the list.

Some actions cannot be undone. Microsoft names commands on the File tab and saving a file as examples. If Word cannot undo, the command changes to Can't Undo. You can still undo many typing and formatting changes even after you have saved, and then save again, as long as you are within the undo limit (Microsoft says Office stores the last 100 undoable actions by default). You do not need to change that limit.

To redo something you have just undone, press Ctrl+Y or F4, or select Redo on the Quick Access Toolbar. Microsoft notes that the Redo button appears only after you have undone an action, and that F4 may need an F-Lock or Fn key on some keyboards. Repeat (also Ctrl+Y or F4) can repeat a simple action such as a paste. If you are on a Mac, Microsoft lists Command+Z for undo and Command+Y for redo.

Undo is not a reason to skip saving. It is a way to fix a recent slip without starting the page over. If Undo does not bring back what you hoped, stop and ask a tutor before you keep clicking — you may have already used a File-tab command that cannot be undone.

lessons.title: Save, name, and reopen a file

sections.title: Why saving matters

blocks.html:
Microsoft says that in Word you must save your document so you can quit the program without losing your work. When you save, the document is stored as a file on your computer or in a network location. Later you can open the file, change it, and print it.

Until the first save, the title bar may show a temporary name. After you save, the title bar shows the name you chose. Saving often is safer than hoping you will remember at the end of class. Undo (Lesson 2) can fix recent slips, but it is not a backup if the program closes or someone else signs in.

On a library computer, save only in the folder staff point you to, and use a practice file — not someone else’s letter. Finding folders in more depth is part of *Everyday Computers and Smartphones*. This lesson stays with Word’s own Save and Open commands, plus Microsoft’s File Explorer tip. A file you never save is like a letter you never put in a folder: it is easy to lose when the session ends. Make saving part of the same habit as typing the first sentence, not a chore you leave until you are packing up. If the power flickers or a session timer signs you out, unsaved words may disappear. A clear name in Documents is the simplest insurance this course can offer you today. Ask staff if you are not sure which folder you may use.

sections.title: Save the first time, then save again

blocks.html:
Microsoft’s steps to save are:

  1. Click the Save button on the Quick Access Toolbar.
  2. If you have saved this file before, Word saves it with the same name and you are done.
  3. If this is the first save, a Save As or “Save this file” window appears (the wording depends on the Word version). Choose a location, type a name in the File name box, and click Save.

Use a clear name you will recognise next week, such as cover-letter-practice or thank-you-note. Avoid a blank name or a string of numbers you will not remember. Many people save into Documents. Microsoft notes that files may also sit in OneDrive or another location, depending on the computer’s setup.

After the first save, clicking Save (or using Save on the Quick Access Toolbar again) updates the same file. sections.title: Select, then use the Font group

blocks.html:
Formatting changes how text looks so a letter or notice is easier to read. Microsoft says you can find most text formatting tools by clicking the Home tab and then choosing from the Font group. First select the text (Lesson 2), then click a button.

Useful Font-group tools Microsoft lists include Font and Font Size; Increase Font Size and Decrease Font Size; Bold, Italic, and Underline; Font Color (the button may use the US spelling *Color* even when you write *colour*); Text Highlight Color; and Clear All Formatting, which removes extra formatting and leaves plain text. There are also Change Case, strikethrough, subscript, superscript, and text effects. You do not need every button today.

Use formatting for a reason. A title might be larger. A date you want someone to notice can be bold. Long stretches of coloured, underlined, or highlighted text are harder to read. Microsoft’s accessibility guide also cautions against using all capital letters and against using too much italic or underline, and it suggests familiar fonts such as Arial or Calibri to reduce the reading load. Colour should not be the only way you show that something matters, because some people cannot see that difference.

If you format the wrong words, use Undo or select the text and click Clear All Formatting. You can apply more than one look at a time — for example Bold and a larger size — as long as the words stay selected. If the ribbon looks cramped on a small screen, Microsoft says Word may compress the controls; look for the Font group on the Home tab, or ask a tutor to point to Bold.

sections.title: Make a bulleted or numbered list

blocks.html:
Lists help a reader scan. Microsoft’s list help says you can start a numbered list by typing 1, a period (.), a space, and some text — Word then starts the numbered list for you. Type ***** and a space before your text, and Word makes a bulleted list. To finish the list, press Enter until the bullets or numbering switch off.

You can also turn existing lines into a list: select the text, then go to Home > Bullets or Home > Numbering. A down arrow beside those buttons shows other bullet styles and numbering formats.

Microsoft’s accessibility guide asks you not to drop a plain paragraph without a bullet or number into the middle of a list, because some screen readers may then miscount the items. Keep a list together, then press Enter until it ends, then write the next ordinary paragraph.

A short “bring” list on a notice, or three steps in a letter, is enough practice. You do not need nested lists or fancy symbols in this course. After the list ends, click in the next ordinary paragraph and keep writing as usual. If bullets will not switch off, press Enter a second time, as Microsoft describes, until the list marker disappears. Save when the list looks the way you want. A numbered list is handy for steps that happen in order; a bulleted list is handy when the items are just a set, such as things to bring.

Microsoft says styles let you format headings, titles, and subtitles quickly, and the accessibility guide says built-in heading styles help people who use screen readers move through a document.

For today, you can still use Bold and a larger size on a short label if you want, and you can build a list. Just know that a real heading in a letter or notice should later use a style, not only bigger letters. Clear All Formatting is there if a page becomes a mix of sizes and colours you did not mean to keep.

Save after you format so you keep the look you chose (Lesson 3). If you are writing a title you already know will be a heading, you can leave it plain until Lesson 5 and apply the style then — that is often cleaner than making it large and bold now and changing it later. The Font group is still the right place for a single word you want to emphasise inside a sentence.

sections.title: A style is more than bigger, bold text

blocks.html:
In Lesson 4 you made text bold or larger from the Font group. That changes how the words look. A style is a ready-made look that also tells Word what the words *are* — a title, a heading, or ordinary body text. Microsoft says styles let you quickly format major elements in your document, such as headings, titles, and subtitles.

Why does that extra meaning matter? Microsoft’s accessibility guide says title, subtitle, and headings are meant to be scanned, both visually and with assistive technology. Built-in heading styles make it easier for someone using a screen reader to understand the structure of the page and to jump from heading to heading. A title that is only large and bold may look the same to your eye, but it may not announce itself as a heading.

Use the built-in Title and Subtitle styles for the title and subtitle of the document, Microsoft says. Use heading styles for the section labels inside the page. Headings should explain what a section is about. Keep each section fairly short — ideally a heading with only a few paragraphs underneath.

This habit also saves you time later. If you pick a different look for headings, Word can update every Heading 1 at once when you use a style set (Chapter 3). You do not get that gift from one-off bold clicks. Think of a style as a label plus a look: the label is what assistive technology can use, and the look is what you see on the page.

sections.title: Apply a heading style from the Home tab

blocks.html:
Microsoft’s steps to apply a style are:

  1. Highlight the text you want to change.
  2. On the Home tab, in the Styles group, pause the pointer over a style to see a live preview in your document. To see the complete list, click the More arrow to open the Styles pane.
  3. Click the style that is most appropriate for your text.

For a main title on a notice or a letter, Heading 1 (or the Title style, if you are labelling the whole document) is the usual starting point. If you add a second-level label under that, use Heading 2, then Heading 3. Microsoft’s accessibility guide says to keep headings in a logical order and not to skip levels — for example, use Heading 1, then Heading 2, then Heading 3, rather than jumping from Heading 3 to Heading 1 and back to Heading 2.

If the preview does not appear when you point at a style, you can still click the style and then use Undo if it is not the look you wanted. Screens differ, and a library copy of Word may show fewer styles until you open More.

After you apply the style, click away from the text and look at the page. The words should look like a heading, and the Styles gallery should show that style as selected when the cursor is in that line. If you applied a style to too many words, Undo and select only the heading line.

sections.title: Margins give the page a quiet edge

blocks.html:
A margin is the empty space between your words and the edge of the paper. Microsoft says that in Word each page automatically has a one-inch margin. You can choose a ready-made setting or define your own.

Microsoft’s steps are: select Layout > Margins, then select the margin configuration you want, or select Custom Margins to define your own. On many computers you will see names such as Normal. A slightly wider margin can make a one-page notice easier to hold and to punch for a binder. Very narrow margins can make a page look crowded and, when you print, risk cutting off text.

You do not need facing-page or binding settings for this course. If Custom Margins looks like a large box of numbers, choose a named preset instead, or ask a tutor. Preview the page later in Lesson 10 before you print, so you can see whether the margins feel right. A notice that will be posted on a board often looks better with the default one-inch edge than with words running to the paper’s trim. Leave room for a binder clip or a punched hole if someone will file the printed page later on.

Screens differ: the Layout tab may appear as Page Layout on some older versions. If you cannot find Margins, ask rather than guessing at columns or section breaks — those tools are outside this basic course.

sections.title: A simple header, with a caution

blocks.html:
A header is a strip at the top of each page; a footer sits at the bottom. Microsoft’s steps to insert one are: go to Insert > Header or Footer, choose a header style, then add or change the text. To edit an existing header or footer, double-click it. To leave, select Close Header and Footer or press Esc. Some built-in designs already include page numbers. To remove a header from a title page, Microsoft says to select it and check Different First Page.

Keep header text short: a document name such as “Hall booking — practice,” or your name on a homework page. Microsoft’s accessibility guide gives an important caution: avoid writing important information only in the header or footer, because those areas are easy to miss for people who use screen readers (they do not scan headers and footers the same way they scan the body). Put titles, subtitles, page-number explanations that matter, and other key facts in the main body with heading styles. The header can repeat something that is already on the page.

That is why Lesson 5 asked you to style the real title in the body. The header is extra, not a hiding place. If you already typed a long sentence only in the header, copy that sentence into the body, apply a heading style, and leave a short repeated label up top. Double-check by clicking in the body: you should still see the title when the header is closed.

sections.title: Add a page number

blocks.html:
On Windows, Microsoft’s page-number steps (opened 10 November 2026) are: double-click in the header or footer where you want the numbers to go; go to Insert > Page Numbering; select Current Position; then choose a style. To move a number that is already there, select it and use Tab to shift it left, centre, or right (if it is flush left, Tab once for centre and twice for right; Backspace moves it back). You can change how the number looks with Home > Font.

Mac and Word for the web use slightly different labels on the same Microsoft page (for example Insert > Page Number on Mac, or Insert > Page Numbers on the web, where you pick a position). If the button you see does not say “Page Numbering,” look for Page Number or Page Numbers, or ask a tutor. This course follows the Windows steps above and does not invent extra menus.

A page number is handy on a letter that might run to a second sheet. On a one-page notice it is optional. Because screen readers may skip headers and footers, do not rely on a header page number as the only way someone knows they are in a long document — but it still helps people who print the pages and stack them.

When you are done, close the header (Close Header and Footer, or Esc) so you are typing in the body again. Save.

sections.title: Word can only check the language it is set to use

blocks.html:
This course uses Canadian spelling, including *centre*, *colour*, *cheque*, and *practise* as a verb / *practice* as a noun. Those are the spellings we ask you to use in practice files. Word will only mark a word as a problem in the language it is using for proofing. If Word is set to another kind of English, it may flag *centre* or *colour* as if they were mistakes — or it may miss a real typo.

Canada’s Skills for Success describe writing as including correct spelling, clear punctuation, and a review step: proofread and correct your writing for grammar and spelling. Word’s checker is a helper for that review. It is not a judge, and this course is not an English-test credential.

Microsoft says you can manage the language or languages that check spelling and grammar. You can set a language for selected text, add a language to Office, and — if you write in more than one language — turn on automatic language detection. You do not need every option today. The everyday path is: select your text (or click in the paragraph), then tell Word which language to use for proofing.

On a shared computer, change the language for your practice document rather than trying to rebuild Office for everyone. Ask a tutor before you download extra language packs. A single practice page set to the right language is enough for this lesson.

We did not find a single required menu label on the Microsoft pages opened 10 November 2026 that we can quote as “English (Canada)” word for word. Look for a Canadian English option if it appears on your computer. If you do not see it, ask a tutor — extra language or proofing tools may need to be installed.

Microsoft also says that if you do not want Word to mark errors in the selected text, you can choose Do not check spelling or grammar for that selection. That is useful for an address block or a name Word does not know. It is not a reason to turn checking off for a whole letter. After you choose a language, click OK (or the matching confirm button on your screen) and look through the page for wavy underlines. Those marks are invitations to look again, not orders to change every word.

If you write in more than one language, Microsoft describes a Detect language automatically check box under Review > Language > Set Proofing Language. If you use only one language, that step is not necessary.

lessons.title: A small table and a picture with alt text

sections.title: A table is for simple facts, not for decoration

blocks.html:
A table organises facts in rows and columns — for example, three time slots and where they happen. Microsoft’s accessibility guide says that, in general, you should avoid tables if you can present the same information another way, such as short paragraphs with headings. If you do use a table, keep it simple and use it for data only. Specify column header information. Do not merge or split cells, nest one table inside another, or leave completely blank rows or columns, because screen readers count cells and can lose their place.

To insert a table, Microsoft’s steps are: choose Insert > Table, then choose how many boxes you want across (columns) and how many down (rows). Two new tabs appear: Design and Layout (Table Tools). On the Design tab, in Table Styles Options, choose Header row. Then click in the first cell of the top row, type the column name, and press Tab to move to the next column.

A good practice table for this course might have two columns and three or four rows: “Item” and “Notes,” or “Time” and “Place.” It is not a spreadsheet. If you need numbers that add themselves up, that skill belongs in *Microsoft Excel Basics*, not here. Keep the table narrow enough to read on a phone screen; Microsoft warns that fixed-width tables can force extra sideways scrolling.

You do not need Total Row, banded styles, or nested tables today. Simple facts, a header row, and clear column names are enough.

sections.title: Pictures need words as well as pixels

blocks.html:
A small picture can help a community notice — a simple photo of a hall entrance, or a logo staff say you may use. Look for Picture on the Insert tab. The next choices differ by version (a folder on this computer, stock images, or other sources). Ask a tutor to point to the control that opens a file you are allowed to use. Do not insert pictures from unknown websites, and do not use a photo of another person without their okay. On a shared computer, use a practice image staff provide.

Once the picture is on the page, it still needs alternative text (alt text) if it carries meaning. Microsoft says alt text helps people with visual disabilities understand pictures and other graphical content. When someone using a screen reader reaches a picture, they hear the alt text; without it, they may only know that a picture is there. Briefly describe the object and its context in one or two sentences. Microsoft says not to start with phrases such as “a graphic of” or “an image of,” and not to repeat the sentence that already sits beside the picture.

If the visual is only decoration — Microsoft’s example is a stylistic border — you can mark it as decorative instead of writing alt text. People who use screen readers then hear that the object is decorative, so they know they are not missing a fact. Prefer real text in the document over words that exist only inside an image. If a picture contains important words, repeat those words in the page itself.

In the Alt Text pane, type one or two sentences that describe the object and its context for someone who cannot see it. Word may generate automatic alt text. Microsoft says you can approve it if it is satisfactory, and you can turn automatic alt text on or off under File > Options > Accessibility. If automatic text appears, read it. Remove leftover comments such as a note that the content may be incorrect, and rewrite anything that does not match the picture.

You can also ask Word to look for missing alt text. Microsoft says the Accessibility Checker runs in the background and can be opened with Review > Check Accessibility. For this basic course, it is enough to add your own short description and to keep the table simple. Save when you are done.

lessons.title: Write a short Canadian letter or community notice

sections.title: Choose a letter or a notice, not a new kind of writing course

blocks.html:
This lesson is about using Word, not about becoming a professional writer. You will open a starter we wrote ourselves and make it look finished: a heading style, a short list, Canadian spelling, and a file you can find again. Longer lessons on tone, workplace messages, and rewriting sentences belong in *Workplace Writing* if your council offers it. A resume cover letter that you would send to an employer belongs in *Job Search and Employment Readiness in Canada*. This page is not legal, career, or immigration advice, and it is not a real booking with a town office.

The letter starter is a sample question about community-hall hours. It includes a place for your name and town, a sample office address, a greeting, two short body paragraphs, and a closing. The notice starter is a sample Saturday market at a community centre, with a “Bring” list. Both files use Canadian spelling on purpose (*centre*, *cheque*, *colour*, *practise*) so you can check proofing (Lesson 7) as you edit.

Pick one file to finish today. You may try both if you have time, but the capstone in Lesson 10 only asks for one polished page. Replace the placeholder lines such as [Your name] with practice words — not your SIN, not a real bank number, and not anyone else’s private details.

sections.title: Build the page with the tools you already have

blocks.html:
Work through the page in a calm order:

  1. Save a copy with a clear name such as hall-letter-practice or centre-notice-practice (Lesson 3) so you do not overwrite the starter by accident.
  2. Give the title a style. On the notice, select “Saturday market at the community centre” and apply Heading 1. On the letter, you may add a short title line such as “Hall booking question” and apply Heading 1, or apply the Title style if that fits. Do not skip heading levels (Lesson 5).
  3. Replace placeholders and keep paragraphs short. Press Enter only when you want a new paragraph (Lesson 2).
  4. Make a list where it helps: the notice already has a “Bring” list you can format with Home > Bullets. In the letter, you could turn two questions into a short numbered list if that makes them easier to scan (Lesson 4).
  5. Check spelling with Review > Language > Set Proofing Language, and look for a Canadian English option if it appears (Lesson 7). Read suggestions before you accept them. Keep *centre*, *colour*, *cheque*, and *practise* (verb) / *practice* (noun).
  6. Optional extras: a simple header with a short repeated label, Normal margins, and a page number (Lesson 6); a tiny table of hours (Lesson 8) only if it helps. Put the real title in the body, not only in the header.

You do not need a picture on the letter. If you add one to the notice, write alt text (Lesson 8). You do not need columns, watermarks, mail merge, or envelopes — those are outside this basic course.

sections.title: Read the page the way another person would

blocks.html:
Before you call the page finished, look at it from the top:

  • Is there a clear heading style on the title?
  • Are the paragraphs easy to scan, with a list where a list helps?
  • Do the Canadian spellings still look right?
  • Did you leave any bracketed placeholder, such as [Date], that you meant to fill with a practice date?
  • If you added a header, is the important title still in the body?
  • Did you save?

Microsoft’s accessibility habits still apply on this short page: use a logical heading, keep a list together, and do not hide key facts only in a header. Skills for Success describes writing as planning who will read the text and then reviewing it. You do not need a long plan for a one-page practice letter — just remember that a town-office sample is for a staff reader, and a notice is for neighbours who may glance at it on a board.

If the words feel awkward, change them in your own voice. Do not copy a real poster or a real letter from someone else. These starters exist so you have original practice text that is clearly marked sample only.

When the page looks right on screen, you are ready for Lesson 10: preview, print if staff agree, and export a PDF.

lessons.title: Preview, print, and export a PDF

sections.title: Preview before you spend paper

blocks.html:
Microsoft’s preview-and-print page shows this path: click the File tab; click Print to see a preview of the layout before anything is printed; review the settings for any properties you might want to change; and when the printer and document settings look the way you want, click Print.

Look at the preview the way you would look at a photocopied page. Are the margins comfortable? Does the heading still show? Is a table cut off at the edge? Did a header collide with the title? If something looks wrong, press Escape or click back to the document (the exact control differs), fix the page, save, and preview again. It is cheaper to fix a heading now than to print three copies that hide the last line.

Ask learning-centre or library staff which printer to use, and whether you should print at all. Some sites prefer a PDF (Chapter 2) so you can email the file or print at the desk. Do not print other people’s documents, and do not print fifty copies of a practice letter. One copy, with permission, is enough to see how the paper looks.

Save before you print. Microsoft notes that some File-tab actions cannot be undone; printing is not the same as saving, and a paper copy does not replace the file on the computer. If the preview looks crowded, try Normal margins again or shorten one paragraph rather than shrinking every font.

sections.title: Save a PDF so the page travels well

blocks.html:
A PDF is a file that Microsoft describes as looking the same on most computers, often with a smaller file size, and useful when you want something that will be read (not edited) and printed — including by a commercial printer. Examples they list include resumes, legal documents, and newsletters. Your practice letter or notice is a gentle version of that idea: a page you can share or print without asking the other person to own Word.

Microsoft also gives an important caution (opened 10 November 2026): many programs, including Word, can open and edit PDF files. Simply sharing something as a PDF is not enough to guarantee that the recipient cannot change it. Do not treat a PDF as a locked legal seal.

To create a PDF from Word on Windows, Microsoft’s steps are: if the file was previously saved, select File > Save a Copy; if it is unsaved, select File > Save As or Save a Copy. Select Browse to choose a location. In the drop-down list, select PDF, then select Save. You can select More Options > Options to customise the PDF. To make the document easier for screen-reading software to read, Microsoft says to select Document structure tags for accessibility. Other options (page range, bookmarks, passwords) exist; you do not need a password for a practice file, and you should not lock staff out of a file they must open.

On a Mac, Microsoft lists File > Save As or Save a Copy, then File Format > PDF. Word for the web can save a basic PDF from File > Print by choosing Save as PDF. This course follows the Windows desktop steps above and notes that other screens differ.

sections.title: Finish the capstone, then take the exam

blocks.html:
You now have the pieces of a basic Word habit: start the program, type and select, save with a name, format with the Home tab, apply a heading style, set a simple page, check Canadian spelling, add a small table or a picture with alt text when the page needs one, and preview before you print or export.

The capstone asks you to finish one page — the letter or the notice — with:

  • Canadian spelling
  • a heading style on the title
  • a short list
  • a PDF export

Print only if staff agree. The capstone is practice and is not graded. After you try it, take the final exam. The exam is the only graded piece. The pass mark is 70 percent (21 out of 30). You have two attempts. The certificate is a sample of completion; it is not MOS, not college credit, and not a promise of work.

If a button on your screen does not match a practice drawing, ask. Word looks a little different on each computer, and this course said that from the first lesson.

sections.title: Capstone

blocks.html:
This capstone sits after Lesson 10. It pulls the course together: you finish one page — the letter starter or the notice starter — with Canadian spelling, a heading style, a short list, and a PDF export.

This is not legal, career, or immigration advice, not a real booking, and not a real community event. Use the sample text we wrote. Do not type a Social Insurance Number, a password, a real bank number, or anyone else’s private details.

### What to build

  1. Open either Word-Basics-Letter-Starter-Sample-Only.docx or Word-Basics-Notice-Template-Sample-Only.docx.
  2. File > Save As (or Save a Copy) with a name such as yourname-hall-letter-practice.docx or yourname-centre-notice-practice.docx.
  3. Apply Heading 1 (or Title) to the real title in the body. On the notice, that is “Saturday market at the community centre.” On the letter, add a short title such as “Hall booking question” if you need one.
  4. Replace placeholders such as [Your name] with practice words. Do not use real private numbers.
  5. Format a short list (Home > Bullets or Numbering). The notice already has a “Bring” list; the letter can turn two questions into a numbered list.
  6. Review > Language > Set Proofing Language and look for a Canadian English option if it appears. Read suggestions. Keep *centre*, *colour*, *cheque*, and *practise* (verb) / *practice* (noun).
  7. Optional extras from earlier lessons: Normal margins; a short header that repeats a label while the real title stays in the body; a tiny table with Header row; a picture with one or two sentences of alt text.
  8. File > Print to preview. Fix and save if something is cut off.
  9. File > Save a Copy or Save As → Browse → PDF → Save. If you see Options, leave Document structure tags for accessibility selected. Do not add a password on a shared computer.
  10. Print only if staff agree. Keep both the Word file and the PDF.

### Self-check / model answer

  • A PDF export exists beside the Word file.
